summary: An older (first-generation) antipsychotic for schizophrenia and for short-term control of severe agitation during psychotic episodes. It has a strong calming effect, but a higher risk of movement side effects and raised prolactin hormone than many newer options. It is not available in the US.
description: Clopixol (zuclopenthixol) is a first-generation antipsychotic used to treat schizophrenia and to quickly settle severe agitation or aggression during psychosis. It comes as tablets, a short-acting muscle injection for sudden agitation (Acuphase), and a long-acting depot injection for ongoing treatment (Depot). It can work very well for reducing hallucinations, delusions and agitation, but it also has real downsides: stiffness, a strong inner restlessness, shaking, sleepiness, dry mouth and constipation, and rare but serious risks like NMS (an emergency with very high fever, rigid muscles and confusion) and dangerous heart-rhythm changes (QT prolongation). It is not available in the United States.
patient_summary: Clopixol can calm psychosis and agitation fast, and sometimes that’s exactly what you need. But it’s not a “light” medicine. There is a real chance of sleepiness and movement side effects, and you’ll need careful monitoring (especially for movement side effects, blood pressure drops and heart-rhythm risk). The depot injection can make a big difference in preventing relapse if daily pills are a struggle.

primary.context: Used for acute symptom control and long-term relapse prevention. Depot formulations can improve adherence and reduce relapse risk when daily pills are inconsistent.
Short-acting IM zuclopenthixol acetate (Acuphase) is used short-term to rapidly settle severe agitation in acute psychotic episodes.

secondary.context: Antipsychotics are not indicated for catatonia and may worsen symptoms and increase NMS risk; treat catatonia directly (often benzodiazepines and/or ECT) before considering antipsychotics.

therapeutic_response.display: Acute agitation: sedation may begin within ~2 hours after acetate injection; schizophrenia symptom improvement is typically noticed over 1-2 weeks with continued gains over 4-6 weeks.

common_adverse_effects.notes: Expect more sleepiness early on, especially after dose increases. If you feel dangerously sedated (can’t stay awake, slurred speech, unsafe walking), that’s a dose/interaction red flag.
Annoying but common. Hydration, sugar-free gum, and oral care help. Tell your clinician if constipation also ramps up.
This one is brutal if it hits. People describe it as “my body can’t stop.” Don’t power through—call your prescriber. Dose adjustments or meds can help.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Tremor: 8-21%; Hypertonia: 5-26%; other movement side effects reported
common_adverse_effects.notes: Stiffness, shakiness, slowed movements—classic typical antipsychotic tradeoffs. The goal is symptom control without turning you into a statue.
Yes, an antipsychotic can still leave you keyed up, especially if a strong inner restlessness is part of it. If your sleep gets worse, talk to your clinician instead of treating it yourself.

serious_risks.risk: A rare emergency (NMS): fever, severe muscle stiffness, confusion, unstable blood pressure or heart rate. This is a medical emergency; get help right away.
Prolonged QT / torsades risk: palpitations, fainting, sudden dizziness—especially with interacting QT-prolonging meds. URGENT evaluation.
Tardive dyskinesia (involuntary mouth, tongue, face or limb movements) that may last after stopping.
Severe dystonia (acute muscle spasms): neck/jaw/eye spasms (oculogyric crisis) can be painful and frightening but treatable.
Blood dyscrasias: unusual infections, fever, sore throat, bruising—needs evaluation (CBC).
Venous thromboembolism: leg swelling/pain, chest pain, shortness of breath—EMERGENCY symptoms.
Hyperglycemia or diabetic ketoacidosis: excessive thirst/urination, confusion, abdominal pain, vomiting—EMERGENCY symptoms.

safety.black_box_warning: Older adults with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics have an increased risk of death and cerebrovascular adverse events (stroke/TIA). Zuclopenthixol is not approved for dementia-related psychosis.

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to zuclopenthixol, thioxanthenes, or any component of the formulation
Acute intoxication with alcohol, barbiturates, or opioids
Suspected or established subcortical brain damage

precautions: Catatonia warning: Antipsychotics are not indicated for catatonia and may worsen symptoms and increase NMS risk.

A rare but life-threatening reaction (NMS): fever, severe muscle stiffness, confusion, swings in blood pressure, heart rate or sweating. Stop the medicine and get emergency care right away if you suspect it.

Heart-rhythm risk (QT prolongation): use caution if you already have a long QT or take other medicines that lengthen it; side effects from the depot injection can last longer because it leaves the body slowly.
Movement side effects: a strong inner restlessness, sudden muscle spasms, shaking, stiffness; the risk rises with higher doses, younger age and older (typical) antipsychotics.
Tardive dyskinesia (abnormal involuntary movements) that may be permanent; the risk rises the longer you take it, with higher total doses and with older age.
Dizziness or feeling faint when standing up, and falls: blood pressure drops can raise fall risk, especially in older adults.
Metabolic risk: hyperglycemia and dyslipidemia can occur; monitor even though this is a typical antipsychotic.
Blood problems: dangerous drops in white blood cells (infection risk) have been reported; blood counts are checked if you have risk factors or symptoms.
Aspiration risk: antipsychotics can worsen swallowing coordination in vulnerable patients; caution in those at aspiration risk.

interactions.mechanism: It should not be used if you are acutely intoxicated or heavily sedated; the sedation adds up and can become dangerous (falls, breathing problems, poor judgment).
interactions.action: Avoid alcohol. If opioids or other sedatives are medically necessary, the lowest doses should be used, with close monitoring and frequent safety checks.

interactions.interactant: QT-prolonging medications (certain antiarrhythmics, some antibiotics, methadone, many other antipsychotics, some antidepressants)
interactions.mechanism: Higher risk of QT prolongation and potentially life-threatening arrhythmias, especially in vulnerable patients.
interactions.action: Review medication list for QT risk, consider baseline and follow-up ECGs, correct electrolytes (K/Mg), and avoid high-risk combinations when possible.

interactions.interactant: Medicines that slow how your body breaks it down (e.g., fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion; some others have a smaller effect)
interactions.mechanism: May increase medication levels and side effects (sedation, EPS).
interactions.action: If combined, monitor closely for EPS/sedation and consider dose adjustments based on tolerability.

interactions.interactant: Other dopamine-blocking meds (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, additional antipsychotics)
interactions.mechanism: Blocking dopamine twice adds up and raises the risk of movement side effects and tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements that can last).
interactions.action: Avoid duplication when possible; if overlap is needed during switching, do it intentionally with a plan and monitoring.

interactions.mechanism: Dizziness and feeling faint when standing up can get worse, raising fall risk.
interactions.action: Monitor blood pressure and symptoms; adjust timing and doses if needed.

interactions.interactant: Anticholinergic (drying) medicines, e.g., diphenhydramine, some bladder medicines, tricyclics
interactions.mechanism: Constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, and confusion can worsen—especially in older adults.
interactions.action: Keep drying side effects to a minimum; treat constipation early; get checked if you have trouble peeing or severe dry mouth.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Mental status and alertness: every visit (sedation, confusion, agitation, psychosis severity).
EPS monitoring: every visit; reassess 4 weeks after initiation and after dose changes; use a formal rating scale at least annually (or every 6 months if high risk).
Tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements): checked every visit for early signs, with a formal tool at least once a year (or more often if high risk)
Vitals and orthostatics: as clinically indicated, especially early in treatment and in older adults (dizziness, syncope, falls).
Weight/BMI: every visit for first 6 months, then at least quarterly; consider waist circumference at baseline and annually.
Glucose (fasting glucose or HbA1c): around 4 months after starting, then annually (more often if abnormal).
Lipids: around 4 months after starting, then annually (more often if abnormal).
Blood count (CBC): when needed; checked closely in the first months if you have had low white blood cells before, including from a medicine
Electrolytes, renal function, liver function, TSH: as clinically indicated (baseline and symptom-driven checks are reasonable).
ECG: consider baseline and follow-up when QT risk factors exist (cardiac history, electrolyte issues, QT-prolonging meds, high doses).
Prolactin hormone: questions about symptoms each visit until stable (sexual problems, period changes, milky nipple discharge, breast growth in men); a level is checked if symptoms appear
Fall risk: evaluate regularly in older adults and anyone with sedation/orthostasis.

Therapeutic drug monitoring (optional): trough level just before next dose; therapeutic reference range reported as 4 to 50 ng/mL; use clinically (adherence/side effect questions), not as the main driver of dosing.

special_populations.pregnancy: Human outcome data for zuclopenthixol are limited. The manufacturer generally advises using it in pregnancy only if the benefits outweigh the risks. As with other antipsychotics, use in the last three months of pregnancy can cause movement or withdrawal symptoms in the newborn (agitation, abnormal muscle tone, shaking, feeding problems, breathing trouble, sleepiness) that may settle on their own or need hospital care. The lowest dose that works is used, avoiding extra medicines when possible; don’t suddenly stop an antipsychotic that is working just because of pregnancy without a plan made with your care team.
special_populations.lactation: Zuclopenthixol is present in breast milk, and the manufacturer has not established that it is safe during breastfeeding. If you are thinking about breastfeeding, have a deliberate talk with your care team about the risks and benefits (baby sleepiness, feeding problems, and monitoring).
special_populations.geriatric: Avoid for behavior problems of dementia or delirium unless non-medicine strategies have failed and the person may harm themselves or others; if used, review regularly and try to stop when safe. For psychosis or schizophrenia starting later in life, lower doses are often enough: start at about 25% to 50% of the usual adult starting dose and raise it slowly, watching closely for dizziness on standing, falls, movement side effects, confusion, and low blood sodium (which can cause confusion, headache or seizures).
special_populations.renal_impairment: The manufacturer gives no formal dose change; one is unlikely to be needed because little leaves through the urine. Use caution with significant kidney problems because it has not been well studied and people may be more vulnerable.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: The manufacturer gives no formal dose change, but caution is needed because the liver breaks down most of it, and liver problems can raise levels and side effects. Start low, go slow, and watch carefully for sleepiness and movement side effects.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Oral bioavailability ~44%; IM oil-based injections release medication slowly over days (acetate) or weeks (decanoate).
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Tablet ~4 hours; acetate/decanoate injections often 24-48 hours (slow-release oil preparations).
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Oral terminal half-life ~20 hours (range ~12-28 hours); decanoate terminal half-life ~19 days.
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensive hepatic metabolism (multiple pathways; CYP2D6 major and CYP3A4 minor involvement is clinically relevant for interaction risk).
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: May be taken without regard to meals (practical guidance).

dosing.titration: Dosing depends on whether you’re treating acute agitation (short-term calming) or schizophrenia maintenance (stability and relapse prevention). Oral dosing is usually divided at first, then may be simplified once stable. The acute IM acetate injection is short-term only; the depot is for ongoing maintenance.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: With chronic psychotic disorders, stopping antipsychotics outright is often not the goal—switching is usually safer if the medication isn’t tolerable or isn’t working. If someone insists on stopping, tapering oral therapy gradually over weeks to months helps you catch early relapse signs and reduces the chance of withdrawal-type symptoms (agitation, insomnia, sweating, GI symptoms, restlessness, rebound psychosis). For long-acting injectables, a “taper” is usually not needed because the medication leaves the body slowly, but you still need close monitoring for relapse as levels drift down over time.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Zuclopenthixol (Clopixol) is a typical antipsychotic used to treat schizophrenia and to manage acute agitation/aggression during psychotic episodes. It’s not a “general calming med” for everyday stress—this is for serious psychotic symptoms and dangerous agitation where safety and stabilization are the priority.
items: {link:condition:schizophrenia:Schizophrenia}: Long-term symptom control and relapse prevention (tablets or depot injection).
{link:condition:acute-psychosis:Acute psychosis with agitation/aggression}: Short-term control of severe agitation during psychosis (tablets or short-acting IM acetate).

items.note: The short-acting injection is often used specifically for rapid calming in acute psychosis.

It felt like my body got heavier—sleep came easy.

quotes: The paranoia eased up, but I felt a little numb.
Less fear, less intensity… but also less spark.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: How fast it works depends on the formulation and what you’re treating.
key_points: Short-acting IM acetate (Acuphase): calming/sedation may begin within ~2 hours; it’s designed for short-term use only (days, not months).
Oral tablets: early symptom shifts may show up over 1-2 weeks, with continued improvement over 4-6 weeks (especially for hallucinations/delusions and overall organization).
Depot decanoate (Depot): built for maintenance; slow release with a long terminal half-life (on the order of weeks), so changes are steadier and longer-lasting.
Acetate and decanoate injections: clinical effects often last 2-3 days (acetate) or weeks (decanoate) due to oil-based slow release.

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Clopixol is used because it can reduce psychotic symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganization) and, in the acute setting, rapidly reduce agitation that can be dangerous. The depot formulation is especially helpful when missed doses are driving relapses—steady medication levels can mean fewer crises and fewer hospitalizations (when it’s the right fit).
sections.metric: Symptom control in schizophrenia + rapid calming in acute agitation
sections.clinical_details: In practice, effectiveness is judged by real outcomes: fewer psychotic episodes, fewer emergency escalations, improved sleep and behavioral control during acute agitation, and better day-to-day functioning. Response varies, and the “cost” can be EPS and sedation—so the goal is always the lowest effective dose with close monitoring.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Do not use for catatonia. Watch for neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), dangerous movement reactions, and QT-related heart rhythm risk—especially with higher doses or interacting meds.
sections.black_box: Older adults with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics have an increased risk of death and cerebrovascular adverse events (stroke/TIA). Zuclopenthixol is not approved for dementia-related psychosis.
other: Catatonia warning: Antipsychotics are not indicated for catatonia and may worsen symptoms and increase NMS risk.
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): rare but life-threatening (fever, severe rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability). Stop medication and seek emergency care immediately if suspected.
QT prolongation/arrhythmia risk: use caution if you have known QT prolongation or take other QT-prolonging medications; depot adverse effects can last longer due to slow elimination.
Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS): akathisia, dystonia, tremor, rigidity; risk rises with dose, younger age, and typical antipsychotics.
Tardive dyskinesia: potentially irreversible abnormal movements; risk rises with duration, cumulative dose, and older age.
Orthostatic hypotension and falls: dizziness and blood pressure drops can increase fall risk—especially in older adults.
Metabolic risk: hyperglycemia and dyslipidemia can occur; monitor even though this is a typical antipsychotic.
Blood dyscrasias: leukopenia/neutropenia/agranulocytosis have been reported; monitor if risk factors or symptoms appear.
Aspiration risk: antipsychotics can worsen swallowing coordination in vulnerable patients; caution in those at aspiration risk.
patient_counseling: If you develop fever + severe stiffness + confusion, that’s an emergency—get medical help immediately (possible NMS).
Tell your clinician if you feel inner restlessness, muscle stiffness, tremor, or jaw/neck spasms—these can be treatable EPS, but they need attention.
Stand up slowly. If you get dizzy or faint, that’s a sign your blood pressure is dropping.
Avoid alcohol and avoid mixing with sedatives unless your prescriber is explicitly guiding it—sedation and safety risks stack up.
If you have heart rhythm history or you’re on QT-prolonging meds, an ECG plan matters.
This medication is not for catatonia—if catatonia is suspected, treatment strategy changes.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Common themes: sedation, dry mouth/constipation, and movement side effects (EPS). Serious but rare risks include NMS, QT-related arrhythmias, and blood count problems.

Dizziness or lightheadedness when standing (orthostatic hypotension)
Sexual side effects and hormone-related effects (prolactin issues)

sections.intro: Zuclopenthixol has additive sedation with other depressants, can worsen QT-related risk when paired with QT-prolonging meds, and has clinically relevant metabolism pathways (CYP2D6 major; CYP3A4 minor) that can matter depending on what else you’re taking.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: With chronic psychotic disorders, stopping antipsychotics outright is often not the goal—switching is usually safer if the medication isn’t tolerable or isn’t working. If someone insists on stopping, tapering oral therapy gradually over weeks to months helps you catch early relapse signs and reduces the chance of withdrawal-type symptoms (agitation, insomnia, sweating, GI symptoms, restlessness, rebound psychosis). For long-acting injectables, a “taper” is usually not needed because the medication leaves the body slowly, but you still need close monitoring for relapse as levels drift down over time.
key_points: Oral discontinuation: taper gradually (weeks to months) when clinically safe, unless stopping is due to a serious adverse effect.
Watch for relapse early: sleep breakdown, rising paranoia, irritability, social withdrawal, agitation, functional decline.
Withdrawal-like symptoms can happen, especially after abrupt stopping (restlessness, anxiety, sweating, insomnia, GI symptoms, dizziness).
Long-acting injectables: the drug washes out slowly, so withdrawal symptoms are less likely, but relapse monitoring is still essential.
Switching strategy: cross-titration and overlap are commonly used; people at high risk of relapse may need overlap until the new med is clearly working.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Dosing depends on whether you’re treating acute agitation (short-term calming) or schizophrenia maintenance (stability and relapse prevention). Oral dosing is usually divided at first, then may be simplified once stable. The acute IM acetate injection is short-term only; the depot is for ongoing maintenance.

adult.agitation_oral_initial: 10 to 50 mg/day PO in 2 to 3 divided doses
adult.agitation_oral_titration: Increase by 10 to 20 mg/day every 2 to 3 days based on response and tolerability
adult.agitation_oral_range: Usual therapeutic range: 20 to 60 mg/day PO
adult.agitation_im_acetate_usual: Zuclopenthixol acetate (short-acting IM): 50 to 150 mg IM as a single dose; may repeat in 2 to 3 days if needed
adult.agitation_im_acetate_additional_dose: Some people may need an additional dose 1 to 2 days after the first injection, then repeat every 2 to 3 days as necessary
adult.agitation_im_acetate_limits: Do not exceed a total of 400 mg or 4 injections during a course; duration should not exceed 2 weeks
adult.schizophrenia_oral_initial: 10 to 50 mg/day PO in 2 to 3 divided doses
adult.schizophrenia_oral_titration: Increase by 10 to 20 mg/day every 2 to 3 days based on response and tolerability
adult.schizophrenia_oral_range: Usual therapeutic range: 20 to 60 mg/day PO
adult.schizophrenia_oral_maintenance_simplify: Once stable, may consolidate to once-daily dosing (often at bedtime) for maintenance when appropriate
adult.depot_test_dose: Zuclopenthixol decanoate (Depot) test dose: 100 mg IM once to establish tolerability; then wait 4 to 10 days before the full therapeutic dose
adult.depot_maintenance: Zuclopenthixol decanoate (Depot): 150 to 300 mg IM every 2 to 4 weeks (adjust to lowest effective dose for symptom control)
adult.depot_higher_doses: In selected patients, doses up to 600 mg every 1 to 4 weeks may be considered based on response and tolerability, with higher adverse effect risk
adult.conversion_acetate_to_oral: After final acetate injection, wait 2 to 3 days before starting oral tablets: 50 mg acetate q2-3d ≈ 20 mg/day PO; 100 mg acetate q2-3d ≈ 40 mg/day PO; 150 mg acetate q2-3d ≈ 60 mg/day PO
adult.conversion_oral_to_depot: May need supplemental oral dosing during transition, then taper: ≤20 mg/day PO ≈ 100 mg depot q2w; 25-40 mg/day PO ≈ 200 mg depot q2w; 50-75 mg/day PO ≈ 300 mg depot q2w; >75 mg/day PO ≈ 400 mg depot q2w
adult.conversion_acetate_to_depot: When initiating depot maintenance, an initial depot dose may be given with the final acetate injection: 50 mg acetate q2-3d ≈ 100 mg depot q2w; 100 mg acetate q2-3d ≈ 200 mg depot q2w; 150 mg acetate q2-3d ≈ 300 mg depot q2w
adult.administration_im: Deep IM injection into the gluteal region; if volume >2 mL, split between two injection sites; acetate and decanoate can be mixed in the same syringe when clinically necessary (per product guidance)
adult.older_adult_start: If initiating in older adults, consider starting at ~25% to 50% of the usual adult initial dose and titrate slowly with careful monitoring (especially sedation, orthostasis, EPS, sodium)

sections.simple_explanation: Think of it like three tools: (1) tablets for day-to-day dosing (and easier fine-tuning), (2) Acuphase injection for short-term emergency calming in acute agitation (days, not months), and (3) Depot injection for maintenance when consistent coverage is needed to prevent relapse.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Use in pregnancy and breastfeeding requires shared decision-making. For older adults, avoid use for dementia-related behaviors unless nonpharmacologic options failed and there’s risk of harm—antipsychotics raise stroke and mortality risk in dementia. In schizophrenia, antipsychotics may still be appropriate in older adults, but dosing should be lower and slower.
sections.pregnancy: Human outcome data for zuclopenthixol are limited. Manufacturer guidance generally advises use during pregnancy only if benefits outweigh risks. Like other antipsychotics, third-trimester exposure can be associated with newborn EPS or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, abnormal tone, tremor, feeding problems, respiratory distress, somnolence) that may be self-limited or require hospitalization. Use the lowest effective dose and avoid unnecessary polypharmacy when possible; don’t abruptly stop effective antipsychotic treatment solely because of pregnancy without a risk-benefit plan.
sections.lactation: Zuclopenthixol is present in human milk, and safe use during breastfeeding has not been established by the manufacturer. If breastfeeding is being considered, this should be a deliberate risk-benefit conversation (infant sedation, feeding issues, and monitoring).
sections.geriatrics: Avoid for behavioral problems of dementia or delirium unless nonpharmacologic strategies failed and the person may harm self/others; if used, reassess regularly and attempt deprescribing when safe. For late-onset psychosis/schizophrenia, lower doses are often sufficient; start ~25% to 50% of usual adult initiation and titrate slowly with close monitoring for orthostasis, falls, EPS, confusion, and hyponatremia/SIADH risk.
sections.hepatic: No formal manufacturer dose adjustment, but use caution because metabolism is extensive and hepatic impairment can increase exposure and side effects. Start low, go slow, and monitor sedation/EPS carefully.
sections.renal: No formal manufacturer dose adjustment; need for adjustment is unlikely because urinary excretion is limited. Use caution in significant renal impairment due to limited study and overall vulnerability.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Mental status and alertness: every visit (sedation, confusion, agitation, psychosis severity).
EPS monitoring: every visit; reassess 4 weeks after initiation and after dose changes; use a formal rating scale at least annually (or every 6 months if high risk).
Tardive dyskinesia: screen every visit for early signs; use a formal tool at least annually (or more often if high risk).
Vitals and orthostatics: as clinically indicated, especially early in treatment and in older adults (dizziness, syncope, falls).
Weight/BMI: every visit for first 6 months, then at least quarterly; consider waist circumference at baseline and annually.
Glucose (fasting glucose or HbA1c): around 4 months after starting, then annually (more often if abnormal).
Lipids: around 4 months after starting, then annually (more often if abnormal).
CBC: as clinically indicated; monitor closely during first months if low WBC history or prior drug-induced leukopenia/neutropenia.
Electrolytes, renal function, liver function, TSH: as clinically indicated (baseline and symptom-driven checks are reasonable).
ECG: consider baseline and follow-up when QT risk factors exist (cardiac history, electrolyte issues, QT-prolonging meds, high doses).
Prolactin: ask about symptoms each visit until stable (sexual dysfunction, menstrual changes, galactorrhea, gynecomastia); check a level if symptoms appear.
Fall risk: evaluate regularly in older adults and anyone with sedation/orthostasis.

Therapeutic drug monitoring (optional): trough level just before next dose; therapeutic reference range reported as 4 to 50 ng/mL; use clinically (adherence/side effect questions), not as the main driver of dosing.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Zuclopenthixol availability varies by country and is not available in the United States. In Canada, common forms include tablets, short-acting IM acetate (for acute agitation), and long-acting IM decanoate (for maintenance).
items: Oil, intramuscular, as acetate (short-acting): 50 mg/mL (1 mL) (Clopixol Acuphase)
Oil, intramuscular, as decanoate (long-acting depot): 200 mg/mL (1 mL) and 500 mg/mL (1 mL) (Clopixol Depot)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Zuclopenthixol is a typical antipsychotic that primarily blocks dopamine receptors (especially D2) in brain circuits involved in psychosis. It also interacts with serotonin (5-HT2) and alpha-1 receptors, which helps explain parts of its clinical profile (calming effect, blood pressure drops) and some side effects.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Clopixol is typically chosen when schizophrenia symptoms require a strong antipsychotic effect, when agitation is severe and immediate calming is needed (Acuphase), or when adherence is a major driver of relapse and a depot option is clinically preferred (Depot). Like other first-generation antipsychotics, it comes with a higher EPS burden, so treatment is a constant balancing act: symptom control vs side effects, with the lowest effective dose and a real monitoring plan. Guideline-level care emphasizes antipsychotic treatment with monitoring for effectiveness and side effects, and individualized selection based on patient factors and preferences.

faqs.a: Clopixol (zuclopenthixol) is used for schizophrenia (ongoing treatment) and for short-term control of severe agitation/aggression during psychotic episodes. It’s a typical (first-generation) antipsychotic—effective, but with higher movement side-effect risk than many newer meds.

faqs.q: Is Clopixol available in the United States?
faqs.a: No. Zuclopenthixol products like Clopixol are not available in the United States. Availability depends on the country and local regulatory approvals.

faqs.q: What’s the difference between Clopixol, Clopixol Acuphase, and Clopixol Depot?
faqs.a: Clopixol is the oral tablet. Clopixol Acuphase is a short-acting IM injection used short-term for acute agitation in psychosis (think: crisis stabilization). Clopixol Depot is a long-acting IM injection used for maintenance treatment—steady coverage to reduce relapse risk when daily pills are hard to take consistently.

The short-acting injection (Acuphase) can start calming severe agitation within a couple of hours. Tablets usually take longer—early changes may appear over 1-2 weeks, with continued improvement over 4-6 weeks for schizophrenia symptoms.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects?
faqs.a: Sleepiness, dry mouth, dizziness, and movement side effects like restlessness, stiffness and shaking. Some people also get constipation, blurred vision, and sexual or hormonal side effects related to prolactin changes.

faqs.q: What is akathisia (a strong inner restlessness) and why do people talk about it so much?
faqs.a: It is a sense of inner restlessness, like you can’t sit still even if you want to. It can feel miserable and can be mistaken for “anxiety” or “agitation.” If it happens, tell your prescriber quickly; dose changes or specific treatments can help.

faqs.q: Can Clopixol cause serious medical emergencies?
faqs.a: Rarely, yes. NMS is a medical emergency (fever, severe muscle stiffness, confusion). Heart-rhythm (QT) problems are also a concern in high-risk situations (certain medicine combinations, heart disease, low blood salts). If you faint, have severe muscle stiffness with fever, or feel dangerously unwell, get urgent help.

faqs.q: Is Clopixol safe in older adults?
faqs.a: It depends on why it’s being used. Antipsychotics should generally be avoided for behavioral symptoms of dementia unless non-medication approaches failed and there’s a risk of harm. For schizophrenia in older adults, antipsychotics can be appropriate, but dosing should start lower and go slower, with careful monitoring for falls, sedation, and EPS.

faqs.q: Can Clopixol be used for catatonia?
faqs.a: No. Antipsychotics are not indicated for catatonia and may worsen symptoms and increase NMS risk. Catatonia is usually treated first with benzodiazepines and/or ECT, depending on the situation.

faqs.q: Do I need lab work or an ECG on Clopixol?
faqs.a: Often, yes, at least a monitoring plan. Clinicians commonly track weight/BMI, blood sugar and cholesterol, movement side effects and tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements), prolactin symptoms, and blood pressure, including when you stand. An ECG is especially important if you have heart-rhythm (QT) risk factors or take other medicines that lengthen the QT interval.

faqs.q: What happens if I stop Clopixol suddenly?
faqs.a: For long-term psychotic disorders, stopping suddenly raises the risk of relapse. Some people also get withdrawal-type symptoms (insomnia, agitation, sweating, restlessness). If the plan is to stop, it’s usually safer to taper the tablets gradually, or to switch to another antipsychotic with a planned, step-by-step changeover. Depot injections wash out slowly, so tapering isn’t usually needed, but watching for relapse is still crucial.
